planting.note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; Lime Mint bears glossy leaves with a sharp lime-citrus scent, popular for cocktails and iced drinks.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Lime Mint bears glossy green leaves with a sharp, bright lime-citrus scent and flavor rather than the classic menthol of spearmint or peppermint, prized for muddling into cocktails, iced tea, and other cold summer drinks where its citrus edge stands out. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Herb Gardening

common_name: Scotch Spearmint (Smooth Sweet Commercial Oil-Production Mint)

planting.note: Propagate from divisions or rooted cuttings rather than seed, since mint cultivars do not reliably come true from seed; Scotch Spearmint is a commercial oil-production cultivar with a smoother, sweeter spearmint flavor than native spearmint.

directions: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade to light sun, ideally in a buried pot or bottomless container to keep the running roots from overtaking the bed. Scotch Spearmint, a hybrid cultivar long grown for commercial mint oil production, offers a smoother, sweeter spearmint flavor with less of the sharper bite found in native spearmint, making it a favorite for candy, gum, and toothpaste flavoring as well as home culinary use. Like other mints it spreads vigorously by both surface runners and underground rhizomes, so most gardeners grow it contained. Water generously through hot weather, harvest often to keep growth tender and bushy, and cut back hard mid-season to renew fresh foliage.

common_name: Magical Michael Basil (Compact Disease-Resistant AAS Basil)

planting.note: Start indoors 4 weeks early or direct sow after last frost; Magical Michael is a compact, disease-resistant 1996 All-America Selections winner well suited to containers.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture. Magical Michael, a 1996 All-America Selections winner, bears dark green leaves on a compact, uniform, notably disease-resistant plant that holds up better against common basil ailments than many older cultivars, an important trait in the humid Gulf South where basil downy mildew and other foliar diseases are frequent problems. Its tidy, container-friendly size and improved disease resistance make it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for a small herb garden or patio pot. Pinch flower spikes as they form to keep the plant producing tender new leaves, and harvest regularly to encourage continued growth.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Herb Production

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Golden Rain bears green foliage irregularly splashed with gold-yellow variegation, grown chiefly as an ornamental accent.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Golden Rain bears needle-like green foliage irregularly splashed with bright gold-yellow variegation, an ornamental departure from the plain green of most culinary rosemary cultivars, grown as much for its bright, eye-catching color in the landscape as for cooking. It needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, performing well in a container, raised bed, or rock garden where its variegated foliage provides color contrast against darker-leaved companions. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Foxtail bears unusually dense, congested, bottlebrush-like foliage giving each stem a distinctive fox-tail silhouette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Foxtail bears unusually dense, tightly congested foliage packed along each stem, giving it a distinctive bottlebrush or fox-tail silhouette unlike the more open, spreading branch habit of most rosemary cultivars, making it a novelty specimen for collectors and a striking textural accent in the landscape. It needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, performing well in a container or raised bed where its unusual form can be appreciated up close. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape and encourage dense new growth.

common_name: Benenden Blue Rosemary (Narrow-Leaf Vivid Deep-Blue-Flowered Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Benenden Blue is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit rosemary with narrow dark-green leaves and especially vivid deep-blue flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Benenden Blue, a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit holder, bears narrow, dark green needle-like leaves and an especially vivid, saturated deep-blue flower display in spring, among the showiest flowering of any commonly grown rosemary cultivar. It needs sharp drainage and full sun to thrive, performing well in a container, raised bed, or rock garden, and its fragrant, flavorful foliage is fully usable in the kitchen in addition to its strong ornamental value. Prune lightly after flowering to maintain shape.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Award of Garden Merit
